_comment: Story scenes. trigger: {event, ...filters} must match a game event (opening, enter_world, talk, visit, interact, challenge, boss_before, boss_after, record, flag). requires/excludes: world flags. once (default true): plays once, remembered as 'scene:<id>'. Lines: s = speaker id (characters.json), t = text. choices.mode: 'explore' = ask as many as you like, then the exit option; 'decide' = pick one (sets flags that change the story). Effects: set (flags), lore (codex ids), quest (start), action (battle | challenge:<id> | ending:<id>). cutscene: steps played before the first line; a line's 'cut': steps played before that line (walk, face, emote, camera, wait, fade, shake, flash, place - see states/cutscene.py). trial_won: fired after the first victory over a Trial monster (id = its monster id).

lines.t: Before the beginning there was the Null. Nothing could be counted, compared or measured - so nothing could be said to exist.
Then five Axioms woke. 'There is one.' 'One can follow one.' 'Equal things stay equal.' 'Between two points, a line.' 'What changes, changes by a rule.'
Wherever an Axiom held, the world became real. That holding force is the NUMERA - and this world is MATHEA.
...Ahem! Sorry, I was reading the old legends out loud again. You must be the new Numera Trainer! I'm Professor Numeris.
Every trainer needs a partner MathMon. Choose wisely - or at least choose quickly, my tea is getting cold.

Welcome to Starter Village! There you are - I've been looking everywhere for you. My lab is the house with the orange roof, up the path to the north-west. Don't mind the smell, that's research. Probably.
Take this: a NUM-LINK. I built it so we can send each other text messages while you explore. I'm hopeless with gadgets that talk.
Mathematical energy! Wherever the Axioms hold, reality can be counted - and counting holds it together. That 'holding' is the Numera.
It flows through five Axiom Roots under the ground. Each region sits on a different Root. That's why the forest grows in spirals and the caves in pairs!
Where Numera pools, it starts repeating itself. A pattern that learns to keep its shape becomes alive. That's a MathMon!
Young ones copy the animals they see. Old, powerful ones stop copying and become... stranger. Living symbols. Shapes. Light. Fascinating, isn't it?
A MathMon's pattern is steadied by understanding. When YOU truly work something out, your partner feels that clarity, and its move lands true.
Guessing makes the pattern wobble. And mistakes? Mistakes are just data! You learn, you try again. That's my motto.

after.t: Behind you, the Counting Stone in the village square flickers. Its carved numbers peel away and drift into the air like ash.
Far to the south-east, something pulses purple above the trees.
The old ruins. It's natural Numera decay, I expect. Yes. Decay. Probably. ...Definitely probably.
Your first mission: win a battle in the Green Meadow grass, east of here. Then head to the ANCIENT NUMBER RUINS and find out what's going on. Carefully!

lines.t: Ah, my favourite trainer! Or my only trainer. Both, really. What's on your mind?
Four of them! The Tallyfolk here, the Order of the Unknown, Euclidia the Kingdom of Form, and the Timekeepers. They all... faded, about a thousand years ago.
Natural decay of the Numera, I've always said. Tragic. Now, have you tried the Mathmart's new potions?
The Numera Seals there keep something sealed. If they're failing... well. Restore them and we'll find out. Three seals: sums, products and parts.
Splendid! My DIVOWL has been practising its division all week.
Num-Link test! Is this on? ...Good. Watch the MathMon in the grass. Healthy ones keep their shape. If one flickers or glitches - that's the instability.
Also: look for the Tallyfolk counting stones in the meadow. Old Abacus in the village would love to hear what they say.
A visitor! I'm Abacus, village historian. I've been studying the old stones for... oh, seventy-three years. Or seventy-two. You tell me - is 1953 to 2026 seventy-three years?
Ha! Testing you. Old habit. The Tallyfolk tested everyone, you know.
The first people to befriend MathMon - by counting WITH them! One stone, one MathMon, one friend. They built the Arch of Sums and the first Seals.
The songs say 'what remains'. Remains of what, I've never worked out. The Professor says it's all just old poetry. Hmph.

options.label: Why did the Counting Stone flicker?

lines.t: It never has, not in seventy-two years. Or three. When a stone forgets its numbers, the songs say, 'the remainder stirs'. Make of that what you will.
Found any new inscriptions? Every record you read goes into that journal of yours - your CODEX. Press TAB and look. History is a puzzle with missing pieces!
The air in the ruins tastes like static. Broken counting arches lean against each other. Somewhere, numbers are whispering.
The Ancient Number Ruins! Careful - those seals are a thousand years old. Find all three. And read anything carved in stone; the Tallyfolk loved leaving notes.
As the Seal of Sums glows again, you notice fresh scratches around its rim - and wet ink on a rune. Someone opened this seal recently.
Recently? That can't... I mean, how curious! Anyway - well solved! Adding and subtracting are opposites: one undoes the other. That's why you can check a subtraction by adding.
The Seal of Products! Multiplying counts equal groups; dividing shares into equal groups. Same idea, opposite direction - just like adding and subtracting.
A fraction is a number of equal parts. The bottom says how big each part is; the top says how many you have. Only parts of the SAME size can be added directly.
Out of the dark beneath the arch uncoils ARITHMORD, the Tallyfolk's Final Sum - its plus, minus, times and divide signs knotted together and crawling with numbers that never add up.
Its pattern is full of remainders! It can't think straight. Every answer YOU work out steadies your partner. Breathe. Check your work. You can do this!
ARITHMORD's tangled signs slowly fall back into order, and the Beast sinks quietly into the dark beneath the arch. On top of the arch, a hooded figure is watching you.
So the forest's guardian is free. Good. That's one.
The figure steps backwards off the arch - and is gone. Beneath the ruins, rock grinds open: a cave, glowing with crystal light.
You did it! The Numera is flowing again! ...Wait. Someone was WATCHING you? Did they say anything?
...Probably a hiker. Lots of hikers in ruins. Now - that cave. The Order of the Unknown's caverns! Go carefully, and send me everything you find.
Have you seen Sums? He's my DIVOWL. He always shares his snacks into equal piles... but since the Counting Stone flickered, he got scared and flew away!
He likes Pine Ridge, north through the pines. If you find a DIVOWL, could you catch him and bring him home? Please?
You're heading to the ruins? Ha! I'll beat the Arithmetic Beast first. My VOLTIX multiplies faster than anyone. Want to test that?
Scared? ...Fine. I'll be right here. Practising. Not that I need to.
You beat the Arithmetic Beast?! ...I was totally going to do that next.
...Okay, fine. That was amazing. I practise my times tables every night, you know. Don't tell anyone.
Crystals grow in pairs here, each one mirrored by another. On the walls, half-finished equations glow faintly, waiting for their missing numbers.

Wait - you came through the ruins? Then you're the trainer who beat the Arithmetic Beast! I'm Dr. Vexa. My old lab is sealed deeper in by three Variable Seals. Warm up with a few battles, then restore them.
The Order of the Unknown! They discovered that an 'x' is a promise: a value exists, even if you don't know it yet. They stored Numera inside those promises.

options.label: How do you store energy in an x?

lines.t: An equation is a balance. Lock Numera on one side, and the x keeps it safe until someone solves for it. Lovely idea. Dangerous idea.
Me? Oh - once. A long time ago. Very briefly. Hardly counts. ...Is that a SPHYNOX behind you? No? My mistake. Carry on!
Solving for x means undoing what was done to it, in reverse order. If x was multiplied then added to, take away first, then divide. Like taking off shoes before socks!
An equation is a balance scale. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and it stays level. Move all the x's to one side first.
Two equations sharing two unknowns! Add or subtract them so one unknown cancels out. The Order called that 'making the pair confess'. Ha!
Behind the last seal, dust has been swept from the floor. Someone has walked here - and not long ago.
A golden scarab turns slowly in the chamber. Its shell is cracked, and dark Remainder leaks through like smoke.
That's no natural corruption. Someone INJECTED Remainder into it. ...Focus. Keep both sides of every equation balanced and you'll be fine.
As EQUINOX calms, the Remainder pouring out of it is pulled across the room - into a glass phial held by the hooded stranger.
You keep freeing them. Every guardian you break open makes this faster for me. Thank you.
Someone who checks her work. Unlike some people you know.
What remains. The Remainder. Every bit the ancients spilled - I'm putting it back where it belongs.
That's exactly what someone should have said twenty years ago.

after.t: She is gone before you can move. Behind the guardian's chamber, a gateway hums to life.
...A phial of Remainder. She's COLLECTING it. From every guardian. That's - that's impossible. Unless someone told her how. ...Go to the Kingdom. Please hurry.

lines.t: Every path here runs dead straight. Obelisks cast shadows at exact angles, and the hedges are trimmed into perfect right angles.

Halt, traveller! ...Ah, a trainer! I'm Sir Hypot, knight of Euclidia. The Dimension Colossus folded our castle into impossible shapes. Restore the three Geometry Seals in the Pillar Court and the keep will open.
Euclidia, the Kingdom of Form! Their buildings could never fall, as long as every angle was exact. They were wiped out by natural Numera decay. A tragedy.
Area counts the squares INSIDE a shape; perimeter walks the edge AROUND it. A 3 by 4 rectangle has area 12 but perimeter 14. Different questions, different answers!
Angles on a straight line make 180 degrees, and so do the three angles in any triangle. The Euclidians carved that into every doorway.
Volume is layers of area: length times width, times how many layers tall. And for right-angled triangles - square the two short sides, add, then square-root!
You read the burnt page again. The handwriting is unmistakable - the same loops as the notes the Professor leaves on the Mathmart's noticeboard.
Professor. I found a log in the Dragon Keep. 'I told the council it was natural decay. - A.N.' Your initials.
When you reach Chronos, I will tell you everything. I promise. Please - just get there safely first.

options.label: Keep it to yourself for now.

lines.t: You fold the page into your bag. Maybe there's an explanation. Maybe there isn't. Either way, the answer is ahead of you.
The keep unfolds like paper. CRYSTALGON - Euclidia's measuring gem, grown into a colossus of facets from too many dimensions - rises, and the room's angles stop adding up.
Trust the rules, not your eyes! 180 degrees in a triangle - in ANY dimension.
The colossus folds itself small and still. The stranger's phial fills again - she is standing in the sundial's shadow.
Three guardians. One left. Then the Engine. Tell the Professor I'm nearly finished - he'll know what that means.
...I know what it means. Go to Chronos. I'll... I'll be ready to talk.
Islands hang in the air, perfectly still. A bird hovers mid-flap. Every clock tower you can see shows exactly 3:14.
...tick... tock... Oh! Someone is still moving in time! I'm Keeper Tick. The Infinite Overlord stopped every clock. Restore the three Time Seals on the isles, then climb the Time Spire.
I haven't been here in twenty years. ...It looks exactly the same. That's the problem, isn't it. Nothing here has moved in twenty years.
You came from the outside! Then you've met the girl in the hood. Vera. Little Vera Tallow. She used to run between these clock towers with her sums.
Her family's village is on the Tock Isles. Frozen at 3:14, the moment the Engine misfired. I'm the only one who kept ticking. Don't ask me why.
Oh - and this. A rusty key. Your Professor dropped it running out of here twenty years ago. I think it opens a drawer he'd rather forget.
Patterns: find the jump between neighbours. For term number n, start at term 1 and add the jump (n - 1) times - not n times!
Time counts in sixties, not hundreds! Count on to the next full hour first, then add what's left. The Timekeepers never got that wrong.
The Seal of Infinity flares - and the hooded stranger is standing beside it. She lowers her hood. A pocket watch hangs at her neck, stopped at 3:14.
My name is Vera Tallow. Twenty years ago I was the Professor's research partner. Did he ever mention me? No. He wouldn't.
We restarted the Origin Engine to cure the fading Numera. One step needed checking. He was sure it was right. He didn't check.
The Engine misfired. The Remainder burst out, and my village froze. My mother. My little brother. 3:14, forever.

options.label: What are you trying to do?

lines.t: Finish the Last Calculation - correctly, this time. Gather every scrap of Remainder and compute the world exactly. No remainder. No errors.
A world where nothing can ever go wrong again. Where no one ever loses their family to one unchecked step. Tell me that's wrong.

options.label: Is the Professor a bad person?

lines.t: He's a coward who became a kind teacher. Both are true. I've hated him for twenty years and I still use the way he taught me to carry a ten.

after.t: Because you're the only one who has answered every question honestly. Climb the spire if you want. I'll be at the Engine. He knows where.

lines.t: You've met her. I promised you the truth, so here it is - no jokes.
I skipped one check. I was proud and tired and sure. Her village froze, and I told the council it was 'natural decay', because I couldn't bear to say 'me'.
I gave up the Engine and became a teacher, so that no student of mine would ever skip a check. 'Mistakes are just data.' I've been saying it to myself for twenty years.
I'm coming to Chronos. It's long past time.
My Num-Link says the Seal of Infinity is restored. And... I can see who is standing next to you.
You found my log in the Keep, didn't you. And you didn't say a word. Thank you for giving me the chance to say it myself.
Everything Vera told you is true. I skipped one check, and I hid it. I'm coming to Chronos. Whatever happens at the Engine, I'll be there.
At the top of the spire coils INFINITY ZERO, the Engine's ancient guardian. Vera has filled it with every drop of Remainder she gathered.
Everything you've learned - every sum, every x, every angle, every pattern. You won't need anything else. I believe in you.
The serpent uncoils and sinks into the floor. Beneath it, a stair of light leads down - to the Zero Point, where every Axiom Root crosses.
At the bottom stands the ORIGIN ENGINE. And Vera, waiting for you.
The Last Calculation begins now. Every scrap of Remainder, every number in Mathea - summed, exactly, forever.
Vera.
Professor Numeris steps off the stair of light, out of breath, glasses on his head.
I came. I should have come twenty years ago. I'm sorry. Not 'mistakes are data' sorry. Just sorry.
...Then help me check it. Every step. Out loud. You too, trainer - the Engine answers to understanding. Show it everything you've learned.
The Engine's dials stop. Every answer checks. And still - at the very bottom of the calculation - something is left over.
A remainder. Even now. Even done perfectly. ...Why won't it come out even?

options.label: Show Vera the ancients' last record.

lines.t: You pull the great lever. The Engine falls silent, and the Seal of the Zero Point closes over it with a sound like a book being shut.
Then my village stays at 3:14. ...At least no one else's will.
She walks away up the stair of light and does not look back. The Professor watches her go for a long time.
Mathea is safe. That's what matters. ...Isn't it?
ENDING: THE SEALED ENGINE. The Numera flows again. Some questions stay unanswered.
It isn't a mistake. When you divide and something's left over, that's where the next count starts. Without a remainder, nothing new could ever happen.
...Like my village. Nothing new. Nothing ever again.
The ancients were wrong to try. So were we. Let's turn it off, Vera. Together. And then I'll tell everyone what I did.
The Engine powers down. Far above, on the Tock Isles, a single clock moves from 3:14 to 3:15.
ENDING: THE OPEN REMAINDER. Time in Chronos has begun to tick again - slowly.
Look - the ancients' last record. And the Professor's journal. They both found the same thing at the very end.
'The count did not come out even, and we called it ruin. We were wrong. What remains is where the next count begins. Keep it.'
Where the next count begins... Then my family isn't stuck at the end of something. They're waiting at the start of something.
Then let's help them start. Not the calculation - the understanding. Check every step. Out loud. Together.
Vera and the Professor work through the night. At dawn, every clock in Chronos strikes 3:15, and a village wakes up yawning, twenty years late for breakfast.
Mistakes are just data. It took me twenty years to learn what that means.
TRUE ENDING: THE REMAINDER THEOREM. Thank you for playing MATHMON.
I've started a new class: 'How To Check Your Work'. Vera is a guest lecturer. She's much stricter than me. The students love her.
There are still MathMon out there no one has met, and records no one has read. Go on - the world's not finished. That's the best thing about it.
Everyone's talking about you. ...Rematch? I've been learning fractions. Don't laugh. They're actually cool.
I'll be here. Practising. Obviously.
Back from the caves already? Don't tell me - you found the Order's equations! Marvellous. Did you, er... find any notes? Old ones? With initials?

options.label: Who was watching me at the arch?

lines.t: A hiker. Almost certainly. Very determined hiker. ...Look, if you see them again, don't follow them alone. Promise me.

options.label: How do I solve for x?

lines.t: Undo what was done to x, in reverse order. 3x + 4 = 19? Take away 4, then share by 3. x = 5. And then CHECK: 3 times 5 plus 4 is 19. Always check.
Ha! Very well!
Euclidia! I always wanted to walk those straight roads. I... never quite managed it. Funny how life goes.

options.label: Did the ancients cause the Unravelling?

lines.t: The Euclidians wrote that? ...Records can be wrong. Scholars disagree. That's - that's what history IS.
He doesn't meet your eyes. He polishes his glasses, which are on his head.
Area is how much carpet; perimeter is how much fence. Carpet inside, fence around. Never mix them up when you're buying carpet.
Of course!
You're in the middle of Chronos and you came back to see me? ...Thank you. I'm all right. Mostly.
The best student I ever had. She checked everything twice. I used to tease her for it. I don't anymore.

options.label: Why does time count in sixties?

lines.t: Very old habit! Sixty splits evenly into 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 - perfect for sharing hours. The Timekeepers loved it.
A good distraction. Let's!
I'm going to the Zero Point. You've done everything I asked and more. The rest is mine to face - but I'd like you there.
'Never complete the calculation'?! Seventy-three years I've read these stones, and I never found the arch's back side. You have sharp eyes.
The Professor always told me the stones were 'just poetry'. Funny. He reads ancient scripts better than anyone alive.
Voltbyte! The Tallyfolk's lantern-keeper. Every lantern-road in the old forest was lit by its arrays - rows times columns, never a spark wasted.
When the Numera faded, its tables got jumbled and it hid in the dark. You reminded it how multiplying works. I think it'll light the paths again.
...Odd. Its charge felt like it had been stirred up on purpose. I'll make a note. A very small note.
Nullshade... a leftover piece of the Null itself! The Tallyfolk wrote their debts into it - minus three, minus seven - so the darkness had a number and couldn't spread.
You kept count of every negative. That's exactly how they held it. Below zero isn't nothing, trainer - it's a direction.
Its chains were cut cleanly, though. Not rusted. Cut. ...Never mind. Probably nothing!
Mycomorph! The Tallyfolk's harvest-keeper. They divided every crop by its rings - halves, quarters, eighths - so nobody ever went hungry.
Unequal shares upset it. You put every fraction back in balance, so the colony can rest under the pines again.
I once tried to share a cake by its rings. Seven pieces, five people. It sulked for a week.
Crystalgon carries the first perfect triangle of Euclidia inside it! Every facet is a measurement - an area here, an angle there.
Remainder had clouded its faces, so every angle in the kingdom came out crooked. You measured true, and Euclidia adds up again.
If you listen closely, it hums at exactly 180 degrees. Don't ask me how you hear an angle.
Chronowl! The Timekeepers' messenger. They talked in sequences - every hoot was the next term in a message.
It was stuck repeating the last message it ever received. By finishing its patterns you told it time can move again.
That last message... 20, 0, 20, 0. A warning. Twenty years ago. ...I need to sit down.
Equinox, the guardian of the Order of the Unknown. Every equation they wrote, it weighed - left side, right side - so the promises inside stayed true.
Someone poured Remainder into it on purpose. That's not decay, trainer. That's sabotage.
You balanced it again, one step at a time. The Order would have liked you. ...So would someone I used to know.
Infermath was the Order's forge. Give it 3x + 2 = 17 and it burns away the 2, then the 3, until only x = 5 glows in the coals.
With no smiths left to feed it, it started melting the tunnels. You gave it real equations again. Hear that crackle? That's a happy forge.
Inverse operations, trainer. Undo what was done, in reverse order. True for forges... and for mistakes.
The Arithmetic Beast was Arithmord all along - the Tallyfolk's Final Sum, holding every calculation of their whole age.
Without the Numera it forgot the order of operations: brackets, powers, multiply and divide, add and subtract... all in a heap. You untangled it one step at a time.
The Tallyfolk sealed it to protect it, not to punish it. Someone else broke those seals. I'm going to find out who.
Galaxion! Euclidia's astronomers mapped the night sky on its back. Every ring of light is a place value - thousands, millions, billions.
One slipped digit and a whole constellation disappears. You put every place back where it belongs.
I counted its stars once. I got to four hundred and twelve and fell asleep. It didn't seem offended.
Sphynox guarded Euclidia's library. No locks, no keys - only logic. Say something true and the door opens.
It doesn't fight to hurt you. It fights to see if you think clearly. Clearly, you do!
It asked me a riddle once. I'm still not sure if 'yes' was the right answer.
Hexabyte... the Timekeepers' biggest mistake. They wanted a garden that grew by powers. It doubled, and doubled, and never stopped.
They froze it in a stopped moment. You understood its powers well enough to calm it - square by square.
Twenty years ago I wrote a formula that doubled too. I should have stopped it sooner. ...That's a story for another day.
Infinity Zero... the guardian of the Engine where all five Axioms meet. Zero and infinity, nothing and everything, in one creature.
Every sum, every x, every angle, every pattern you've learned - it tested all of them. And you were ready.
Thank you, trainer. Not for defeating it. For understanding it. That's what the Engine always needed.
